the.summary: Russian has no articles, so ask one question before every noun: do both of us know which one? If yes, it takes the.

rules.title: Both sides know which one
rules.body: Something already mentioned, visible, or the only one in the situation takes the. First mention takes a; every later mention takes the.

examples.bad: I opened a PR. Can you review PR?
examples.good: I opened a PR. Can you review the PR?

rules.title: A noun followed by of
rules.body: A noun narrowed down by an of-phrase is specific, so it takes the. This is your most frequent the-pattern.

examples.bad: working on balance of supply and demand
examples.good: working on the balance of supply and demand

rules.title: The only one: main, overall, same, first, best
rules.body: Words that make a noun unique pull in the: the main goal, the overall plan, the same bug, the first release, the best option.

examples.good: The main goal is to improve

examples.bad: Overall goal is to ship it
examples.good: The overall goal is to ship it

rules.title: Names that need the
rules.body: Country names with a common noun or an abbreviation take the: the UK, the US, the EU, the Netherlands. Languages take no article, but the English language does.

examples.good: work on the English language / work on my English

rules.title: Fixed phrases
rules.body: Some phrases are frozen with the: lay the foundation, in the X domain, on the other hand, at the same time, in the end.

rules.title: When not to use the
rules.body: Plural and uncountable nouns in a general sense take no article: Engineers like clean code. Experience matters.

examples.bad: The engineers like the clean code.

a-an.summary: A singular countable noun can never stand alone. If it is not the, it is a or an.

rules.title: Singular countable nouns need an article
rules.body: Roles, things and events counted one at a time need a/an: as an engineer, as a volunteer, an opportunity, a frontend and a backend. Russian «работаю инженером» hides it.

examples.good: improve even further as an engineer
with a frontend and a backend

rules.title: a or an goes by sound, not letter
rules.body: an before a vowel sound: an English course, an MR (em-ar), an hour, an API. a before a consonant sound: a user (you-ser), a unique id, a URL.

rules.title: No a/an with plurals or uncountables
rules.body: Plural nouns and uncountable nouns (information, advice, feedback, experience as skill) never take a/an.

examples.bad: I had an experience with big-scale operations
examples.good: I have experience with large-scale operations

rules.title: One of many
rules.body: Use a when the thing is one of several of its kind, even if you know which one you mean.

prepositions.summary: Prepositions do not translate. Learn each one together with the word that owns it.

rules.title: Where you work
rules.body: in a team, in the X domain, at a company, on a project, on the backend.

rules.title: Words that own their preposition
rules.body: foundation for, depend on, responsible for, interested in, good at, okay at (skills). discuss and explain take no preposition.

examples.bad: laid the foundation as to what

rules.title: Time
rules.body: on Monday, on 1 October, in October, in 2026, at 5 pm, for two years (duration), since 2021 (start point).

examples.bad: I work here since two years
examples.good: I have worked here for two years

verbs.summary: Pick the time frame first, then the form. would and could belong to the past or the imagined, not to plans.

rules.title: Real conditions use will
rules.body: if + present, will + verb. would is for imagined situations: if I had time, I would.

examples.bad: if I make mistakes you would stack them
examples.good: if I make mistakes, you will log them

rules.title: Purpose after an instruction
rules.body: After a present or imperative verb, so that takes present, will or can: extend it so that we work on it.

examples.bad: extend the file so we would also work on it
examples.good: extend the file so that we also work on it

rules.title: Present perfect for what is still true
rules.body: Experience you still have and situations that started in the past and continue: I have experience with, I have worked here since 2021.

examples.bad: I had an experience with Kafka

rules.title: need + to or a noun
rules.body: need to do / need a noun. need + -ing is passive: the code needs refactoring = someone must refactor it.

examples.good: if I need speaking practice / if I need to practise speaking

structure.summary: English wants every part of a sentence to match its partner: lists, pairs and modifiers.

rules.title: Lists end with and
rules.body: Two items: A and B. Three or more: A, B, and C.

examples.good: with a frontend and a backend
in system design and maintainable code

rules.title: Parallel pairs
rules.body: both A and B, either A or B, and items joined by and share one grammatical form.

examples.bad: helping them launch and designing a systems
examples.good: helping them launch and design systems

examples.bad: both grow as Engineer and where I could be useful
examples.good: both grow as an engineer and be useful

rules.title: Noun before noun is singular
rules.body: A noun used as a modifier stays singular: mistake count, error rate, user base, a five-year plan.

rules.title: Who is doing the -ing?
rules.body: An -ing phrase attaches to the subject of the sentence. If the subject cannot do it, add a real subject.

examples.bad: My profile is Golang, working at startup teams
examples.good: My background is Go, and I work in startup teams

punctuation.summary: Three habits fix most of it: it's vs its, a comma after an opening clause, no comma before that.

rules.title: it's or its
rules.body: it's = it is / it has. its = belonging to it. Read it aloud as «it is»: if that works, write it's.

rules.title: Comma after an opening clause
rules.body: When a sentence starts with if, when, whenever, because or after, put a comma where the main clause begins.

examples.bad: If I make mistakes you will log them
examples.good: If I make mistakes, you will log them

rules.title: Two full sentences joined by and
rules.body: Put a comma before and/but when both sides could stand alone.

examples.bad: This took me one month and my work laid the foundation
examples.good: This took me one month, and my work laid the foundation

rules.title: No subjectless sentences in prose
rules.body: Chat drops I; letters and cover letters keep it.

lexis.summary: Translate ideas, not words. When a phrase comes to mind in Russian first, check the collocation.

rules.title: Calques from Russian
rules.body: сильные стороны → strengths; со всех сторон → from every angle; делать исследование → do research; решить проблему → solve a problem.

examples.bad: work on English from all sides
examples.good: work on my English from every angle

rules.title: Words that sound right but mean something else
rules.body: profile → background (career); shareholders (own shares) vs stakeholders (care about the outcome); cleanliness (hygiene) → clean code; stack (pile up) → log, collect.

rules.title: Collocations
rules.body: large-scale (not big-scale), a growing user base, run exams, prospective students, sound like a fun next step.

style.summary: Say it once, plainly, with the same name for the same thing.

rules.title: Cut what repeats
rules.body: new and incoming, both and at the same time: one word is enough.

rules.title: Business email register
rules.body: Hello Jane, (comma, not !). Sign-off and name on separate lines. Small numbers in words: one month.

spelling.summary: Most slips are doubled or dropped letters in long words. Slow down on -ies, -ing and -ment.

rules.title: Doubled and dropped letters
rules.body: opportunities, working, development, environment, necessary.
